title: Surviving the fault: heat, short circuits, breaking capacity

interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the Cmax dot cross the 1.5 mm² cpc's heat limit near 0.46 Ω, before the Cmin dot does, when you drag Zs down and more fault current flows.
interactive.title: The heat a conductor can take
interactive.whatAmILookingAt:
Eleven screens, with Back and Continue, on the heat a fault puts into a conductor and the biggest fault a device must break.

Screen 1, Do you still have it? The question: “A circuit's Zs is 0.50 Ω. Which fault current do you put into S = √(I²t) ÷ k to check its cpc can take the heat?” Three choices, in this order: “437.00 A: 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.50”; “506.00 A: 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.50”; “460.00 A: 230 ÷ 0.50”. Right: “Still there.” Then the working, 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.50 = 506.00 A. The supply can rise to 253 V. More voltage pushes more current round the same loop, and more current means more heat. A line on each slip, then two buttons: Refresh the why (screen 2) and Skip to the practice (screen 6). Wrong, 437.00 A: “That is Cmin. It gives the smallest current, which decides whether the breaker opens in time. The heat check wants the largest.” Wrong, 460.00 A: “The supply can rise to 253 V. Cmax, 1.1, allows for that. The heat check wants the largest current.” Then the right working, and on to screen 2.

Screen 2, What it is for. “A fault current heats every conductor it flows through until the device opens. A fault that clears quickly gives the heat no time to leave. Copper that gets too hot damages its insulation. So three checks follow Zs. The cpc must take the heat of an earth fault. The live conductors must take the heat of a short circuit. And each device must be able to break the biggest fault where it sits, unless a device upstream covers it.” In red, what goes wrong if it is skipped: “A cpc that passes on Zs can still get hot enough to damage its insulation before the breaker opens. A device asked to break more current than it is rated for may destroy itself.”

Screen 3, The why: the heat a cpc can take. Said once at the top: “Take the immersion heater from lesson 6. Its cpc is 1.5 mm² in 70 °C thermoplastic cable, so k is 115. A 16 A type B breaker protects it. It opens within 0.1 s once the fault current reaches 80 A.” The picture: a plot of the heat put in, I²t in A²s, against fault current from 0 to 1300 A. The curve is I² × 0.1, the heat put in during the breaker's 0.1 s. A level line crosses it at 29756 A²s, labelled “What 1.5 mm² can take: k²S²”. Two dots sit on the curve: Cmin, at 230 × 0.95 ÷ Zs, and Cmax, at 230 × 1.1 ÷ Zs. A dot turns red above the line. Under the plot, a bar shows the smallest cpc that copes at the Cmax current, against a mark at 1.5 mm².

The control: a slider, Zs of the circuit, 0.20 to 1.00 Ω in steps of 0.002 Ω, opening on 0.646 Ω. The readouts: fault current at Cmin, fault current at Cmax, and the smallest cpc, S = √(I²t) ÷ k at the Cmax current. The words beside it: “A fault heats the copper faster than the heat can leave it. So the heat stays in the conductor while the fault lasts. The heat is I² × R × t. Halve the area and the resistance doubles, with half the copper to warm. So the temperature climbs four times as fast, which is why the area is squared. k sums up the copper, the insulation and the temperatures it starts at and must not pass. The conductor survives if the fault's I²t is no more than k²S². Turn that round and the smallest area is S = √(I²t) ÷ k.”

What he sees. At 0.646 Ω: Cmin 338.24 A and Cmax 391.64 A. At Cmax the heat is 15338 A²s, under the line. The smallest cpc is 1.08 mm², so 1.5 mm² holds. Drag Zs down, as if the run were shorter or nearer the origin. Both dots climb the curve, because a smaller loop lets more current through. The Cmax dot always sits higher, so it crosses the line first, near 0.46 Ω. The Cmin dot crosses near 0.40 Ω. At 0.43 Ω the Cmin current is 508.14 A and the smallest cpc 1.40 mm², a pass. The Cmax current is 588.37 A, the heat 34618 A²s and the smallest cpc 1.62 mm², a fail. The words under it: “Lesson 6 wanted the smallest current, to be sure the breaker opens in time. The heat check wants the largest, because more current puts in more heat in the same 0.1 s. One Zs, two currents, two questions. The same sum turned round gives the live conductors' time in a short circuit: t = k²S² ÷ I². If that is longer than the device takes, the cable holds out.” The prompt above the picture: “Drag Zs down and watch the two dots.” Read: at 0.646 Ω the Cmax current is 391.64 A and the cpc needs 1.08 mm², so 1.5 mm² holds. At 0.43 Ω the Cmin current asks for 1.40 mm², a pass, but the Cmax current asks for 1.62 mm², a fail. Still: the slider at 0.43 Ω.

Screen 4, Check. “A 32 A type C breaker protects a circuit with Zs 0.38 Ω. Its cpc is 2.5 mm² in 70 °C thermoplastic cable, so k is 115. It is a final circuit, so 0.4 s is allowed. At the Cmax current, 665.79 A, the breaker opens within 0.1 s. What is the smallest cpc that copes?” Choices: “1.83 mm²: the Cmax current for 0.1 s”; “3.66 mm²: the Cmax current for 0.4 s”; “1.58 mm²: the Cmin current for 0.1 s”. Right, the first: “t is how long the device takes at that current. √(665.79² × 0.1) ÷ 115 = 1.83 mm², so the 2.5 mm² cpc holds.” Wrong, the second: “0.4 s is the longest time allowed, not how long the breaker takes. Using it fails a cpc that is fine.” Wrong, the third: “That is the Cmin current, 575.00 A. It is the smaller current, so it puts in less heat than the fault can.”

Screen 5, Worked example, a line at each press. The prompt: “Work each step yourself first, then press Show.” First, the heater's cpc from lesson 6: “15 m of 1.5 mm² 70 °C thermoplastic singles in conduit, with a 1.5 mm² cpc. A 16 A type B breaker. Zs is 0.646 Ω.” The lines: Cmin current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.646 = 338.24 A. That is over the breaker's Ia, 80 A, so it opens within 0.1 s. Cmax current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.646 = 391.64 A. The breaker still opens within 0.1 s. k for the cpc is 115. S = √(391.64² × 0.1) ÷ 115 = 1.08 mm². That is under 1.5 mm², so the cpc holds. Second, a short circuit on the live conductors: “A single-phase circuit in 2.5 mm² twin and earth, 90 °C thermosetting, with a 1.5 mm² cpc. It runs 25 m. A 20 A RCBO protects it, opening within 0.1 s at 100 A. The short-circuit current at the origin is measured as 300 A.” The lines: Ze(l/n) = 230 ÷ 300 = 0.767 Ω. That is the supply's own loop, line to neutral. R1+Rn = 14.82 × 1.28 × 25 ÷ 1000 = 0.474 Ω. Zs(l/n) = 0.767 + 0.474 = 1.241 Ω. Least current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 1.241 = 176.07 A. That is over 100 A, so the RCBO opens within 0.1 s. Greatest current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 1.241 = 203.87 A. k for 90 °C thermosetting copper is 143. t = 143² × 2.5² ÷ 203.87² = 3.08 s. The conductors can carry it for 3.08 s, and the RCBO opens within 0.1 s. So they are safe. A note under the lines: “You may have 341.4 A, 395.3 A, 0.93 mm² and 1.08 mm² written down for the heater. For the short circuit you may have 0.76 Ω, 0.47 Ω, 1.23 Ω, 177.6 A, 205.6 A and 3.02 s. Those figures were rounded down partway through. Both passes stand.” Read: the heater's Cmax current is 391.64 A, so its cpc needs 1.08 mm², under the 1.5 mm² fitted. In the short circuit the greatest current is 203.87 A. The 2.5 mm² conductors can carry it for 3.08 s, far longer than the 0.1 s the RCBO takes.

Screen 6, Section A, question 2 (c). The scenario panel, and parts 1(c), 2(a) and 2(b) carried forward. Then, said once: “The motor circuit's cpc is 2.5 mm², in the same conduit as the 90 °C thermosetting singles, so k is 143. Zs at the starter is 0.366 Ω. That rests on the practice 0.15 Ω at DBP2.” The question: “(c) Determine, for the motor circuit, whether the copper circuit protective conductor satisfies the thermal constraints under fault conditions. First, the minimum cpc size.” A typed answer, part 2c: the Cmax current is 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.366 = 691.26 A. That is past 250 A, so the 25 A type C opens within 0.1 s. S = √(691.26² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 1.53 mm². Accepted too: 1.51 mm², from Zs taken as 0.37 Ω. Slips: 1.32 mm², “You used the Cmin current. The heat check wants the largest current, at Cmax.” 3.06 mm², “You used 0.4 s. That is the longest time allowed. At 691.26 A the breaker opens within 0.1 s.” 1.90 mm², “115 is the k for 70 °C thermoplastic. These are 90 °C thermosetting, so k is 143.” After two misses, the working. Then the judgement: “1.53 mm² is under the 2.5 mm² fitted, so the cpc satisfies the thermal constraints.” One line under it: “The starter-to-motor leg, on the practice 3.0 m, has Zs 0.459 Ω at the motor. 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.459 = 551.20 A, so S = √(551.20² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 1.22 mm². Its 1.5 mm² cpc holds too.”

Screen 7, Section A, question 2 (e). Part 2(c) carried forward. First the rule: “Every device must break the biggest fault current where it sits. That current is IPF, the larger of the earth fault current and the short-circuit current. The device's breaking capacity, Icn, is marked on it, usually in a small box. The rule is IPF ≤ Icn. Assume the showroom's stated 4.6 kA is a fault across all three lines at the origin. That is the biggest fault there.” The question: “(e) Determine the least rated short-circuit breaking capacity (Icn) for the circuit-breakers in the MDB.” A typed answer, part 2e: 4.6 kA. Slips: 2.3 kA, “That is 230 ÷ 0.1, one line to earth at 230 V. A fault across all three lines is bigger, and the stated 4.6 kA covers it.” 2.53 kA, “That is one line to earth at Cmax. The stated 4.6 kA is bigger, so it sets the device.” 2.19 kA, “That is the Cmin earth fault, the smallest. Breaking capacity is checked against the biggest.” After two misses, the working. Then: “A breaker marked 6 kA passes. One marked 4.5 kA does not. Why is 4.6 kA about twice 230 ÷ 0.1? In a fault across all three lines, the neutral carries no current. So the fault current meets one line's impedance, not a line and a return. That roughly halves the loop and doubles the current. A common rule estimates it by doubling the line-neutral figure.[^52] That rule overstates the real current. For Icn, that is the safe way round. A lower Icn is allowed only where a device on the supply side has the breaking capacity needed.[^45]”

Screen 8, Section A, question 3 (f). Parts 3(b) and 3(e) carried forward. Then, said once: “Assume the DBL2 submain is four-core 4 mm² 90 °C thermosetting XLPE/SWA cable, 17.0 m on plan. A 10 A type C breaker at the MDB protects it. The armour is its cpc. The cable size and the breaker are practice values until lesson 8 sizes them. The maker gives 4.61 mΩ/m for each core and 6.8 mΩ/m for the armour, both at 20 °C, and an armour area of 22 mm². Use the 1.28 multiplier on both. The armour runs a little cooler than the cores, so that errs on the safe side. Take k for the steel armour as 46.[^24] That is a practice value. On a real job, read k from Table 54.4.” The words: “SWA armour can be the cpc, as long as a calculation justifies it. This is that calculation.” The question: “(f) Determine the minimum cross-sectional area the armour needs to serve as the DBL2 submain's cpc.” A typed answer, part 3f: R1+R2 = (4.61 + 6.8) × 1.28 × 17.0 ÷ 1000 = 0.248 Ω. Zs at DBL2 = 0.1 + 0.248 = 0.348 Ω. Cmin current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.348 = 627.87 A. That is far past 100 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s. Cmax current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.348 = 727.01 A. S = √(727.01² × 0.1) ÷ 46 = 5.00 mm². Accepted too: 4.99 mm², from unrounded working. Slips: 1.61 mm², “143 is copper's k. Steel armour has a far lower k, 46 here.” 4.32 mm², “You used the Cmin current. Use Cmax for the heat.” 5.92 mm², “You left out the 1.28 multiplier. The conductors are warm when the fault comes.” After two misses, the working. Then the judgement: “The armour is 22 mm², far more than 5.00 mm². So it is justified as the cpc.” One line under it: “A cross-check from the maker: the armour is rated 1.0 kA for 1 s. The same I²t over 0.1 s is 1.0 × √10 = 3.16 kA, well above 727.01 A. Carry Zs at DBL2, 0.348 Ω, into lesson 8.”

Screen 9, Section B: “Explain the difference between a suitable cpc and a minimum cpc.” Written, marked against five points, any three of which make a full answer. One more go, then the model answer.

Screen 10, Section A, changed numbers. “A single-phase circuit is wired in 4 mm² twin and earth, 90 °C thermosetting, 30 m long. A 32 A type B breaker protects it, opening within 0.1 s once the current reaches 160 A. The short-circuit current at the origin is 500 A. Use 9.22 mΩ/m for the line and neutral together, and the 1.28 multiplier. Determine whether the breaker protects the live conductors in a short circuit. First, how long can they carry the greatest short-circuit current?” A typed answer: Ze(l/n) = 230 ÷ 500 = 0.460 Ω. R1+Rn = 9.22 × 1.28 × 30 ÷ 1000 = 0.354 Ω. Zs(l/n) = 0.460 + 0.354 = 0.814 Ω. Least current = 230 × 0.95 ÷ 0.814 = 268.43 A, over 160 A, so the breaker opens within 0.1 s. Greatest current = 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.814 = 310.81 A. t = 143² × 4² ÷ 310.81² = 3.39 s. Slips: 4.54 s, “You used the least current. The heat check uses the greatest.” 0.85 s, “Square the area as well: k² × S².” 2.78 s, “You left out the 1.28 multiplier.” After it: “3.39 s is far longer than the 0.1 s the breaker takes. So the live conductors are protected.”

Screen 11, Keep this: the summary card, then Finish the lesson.

On every screen, each line is worked from the rounded figures shown before it. Each screen that uses a practice value says so.
interactive.ignores: The plot holds the breaker's time at 0.1 s at every current on it. A real breaker often opens faster at high currents and limits the energy it lets through, so 0.1 s is an upper bound. The maker's let-through figure is the better number where you have it. The plot moves Zs on its own, as if the run changed, while the cpc stays 1.5 mm². The heat is taken to stay in the conductor for the whole fault. That holds for faults that clear quickly, and is why the sum is not used beyond 5 s.

explain.text:
A fault current heats every conductor it flows through until the device opens. A conductor survives if the heat the fault puts in, I²t, is no more than it can take, k²S². So the smallest safe area is S = √(I²t) ÷ k. Turned round, the time a conductor can carry a current is t = k²S² ÷ I².

A fault that clears quickly gives the heat no time to leave the copper. The heat is I² × R × t. Halve the area and the resistance doubles, with half the copper to warm. So the temperature climbs four times as fast, and the area comes in squared. k sums up the copper, the insulation and the temperatures it starts at and must not pass. For copper in 90 °C thermosetting cable, k is 143.[^22] Steel armour has a far lower k, so armour needs much more area.

One Zs gives two fault currents, because the supply voltage varies. Lesson 6 took the smallest, at Cmin, to be sure the device opens in time. The heat check takes the largest, at Cmax, because more current puts in more heat in the same time. For t, use how long the device takes at that current, read from its curve. The 0.4 s or 5 s allowed is a limit, not the time it takes. The sum holds for faults that clear within 5 s.[^9] Last, each device must break the biggest fault where it sits: IPF ≤ Icn. IPF is the larger of the earth fault current and the short-circuit current. A device with a lower Icn is allowed only when one upstream has the breaking capacity needed. This picture is simplified. It takes the breaker's time as 0.1 s, an upper bound, and a real breaker is often faster.

**Check the heat at the Cmax current for the time the device really takes, and normally give each device an Icn of at least the fault level where it sits.**

analogy.text: Think of a soldering iron on a cable lug. A thin tail gets hot fast. A heavy lug soaks up the heat. Hold the iron on twice as long and twice the heat goes in. The lug is fine if you take the iron off before it gets too hot. The iron is the fault current, the time it stays on is t, the lug's size is S, and taking the iron off is the device opening.
analogy.breaks: An iron's heat flows in from outside and spreads through the metal. Fault heat is made inside the copper itself, as I²R. And it grows with the square of the current, so a little more current makes a lot more heat.

practice.text:
- Work Zs to the far end of the circuit, hot, as in lesson 6.
- Work the largest fault current: 230 × 1.1 ÷ Zs.
- Read the device's time at that current from its curve. A breaker past the top of its instant-trip band opens within 0.1 s. For a type C that is 10 × In.
- Take k for the cpc's material and insulation from Tables 54.2 to 54.6.
- Work S = √(I²t) ÷ k. The cpc fitted must be at least that.
- For the live conductors, work Zs(l/n) from the short-circuit current at the origin. Then t = k²S² ÷ I², with k from Table 43.1. It must be longer than the device's time.
- Check each device's Icn against IPF where it sits. Its breaking capacity should normally be at least the largest prospective fault current at that point.[^43]

**Rule of thumb:** with t at 0.1 s, the smallest cpc is the Cmax current × 0.316 ÷ k.

**Worked example:** the showroom motor circuit, on the practice 0.15 Ω at DBP2. Zs at the starter is 0.366 Ω. The Cmax current is 230 × 1.1 ÷ 0.366 = 691.26 A. S = √(691.26² × 0.1) ÷ 143 = 1.53 mm². The 2.5 mm² cpc holds.

**Common mistakes**
- Using the Cmin current. It is the smaller current, so it understates the heat.
- Putting the 0.4 s or 5 s allowed in for t. Use the device's time at that current.
- Using copper's k for steel armour.
- Checking Icn against one line to earth when the three-phase fault is bigger.
- Taking Table 54.7's cpc as proven without the heat check.

b1.q: Explain the difference between a suitable cpc and a minimum cpc.

points.text: A suitable cpc is the size Table 54.7 gives from the line conductor. Below 16 mm² that is the same size as the line.
The minimum cpc is the smallest size that still passes the heat check, S = √(I²t) ÷ k. It may be smaller than the suitable one.
points.cite: Flowchart note 2 and steps 18, 19; slides p.58

points.text: To find it, choose a smaller cpc and redo the steps from R1+R2 to the heat check. When the worked minimum comes out bigger than the size chosen, the next size up is the minimum.
A smaller cpc raises R1+R2 and Zs. So Zs must still be within the device's maximum, and the fault current must still open it in time.
The heat check uses the largest fault current, at Cmax, the device's time at that current, and k for the cpc's material and insulation.

summary.title: Surviving the fault: heat and breaking capacity
summary.for: A fault heats every conductor it flows through until the device opens. Check that the cpc and the live conductors can take that heat. Check that each device can break the biggest fault where it sits, or is backed up by one that can.
summary.rule:
Fault current for the heat check = Uo × Cmax ÷ Zs, with Cmax 1.1
cpc: S = √(I² × t) ÷ k, and the cpc fitted must be at least S
Live conductors: Zs(l/n) = Ze(l/n) + (R1+Rn), with Ze(l/n) = 230 ÷ PSCC
Then t = k² × S² ÷ I², which must be longer than the device takes
Breaking capacity: IPF ≤ Icn, with IPF the larger of PEFC and PSCC

t is the device's time at that current, not the 0.4 s or 5 s allowed. The sum holds up to 5 s.
k: 115 for a 70 °C thermoplastic copper cpc in the cable, 143 for 90 °C thermosetting. Steel armour is far lower.
SWA armour may be the cpc when a calculation justifies it.

traps.text: Using the Cmin current for the heat check. It is the smaller current, so it understates the heat.
Putting the 0.4 s or 5 s limit in for t. Use the device's time at that current.
Using copper's k for steel armour.

traps.text: Checking Icn against one line to earth when the three-phase fault is bigger.
Taking Table 54.7's cpc as proven. A suitable cpc and the minimum cpc are not the same thing.
